scenes.text: Here's a surprise. The chips made for video games now power almost every AI you use. [1] Companies spend billions buying them, and wait months to get them. [2] Why does AI need GPUs? Let's find out.

Let's compare two chips. [1] A CPU has a few very powerful cores. It's like a handful of professors, great at complex tasks, one after another. [2] A GPU has thousands of simpler cores. It's like a stadium full of students, each doing a simple sum, all at the same time.

And AI is mostly simple math, repeated billions of times. [1] Every layer of a neural network multiplies big grids of numbers, called matrices. [2] Each multiply is simple, and they can all run side by side. [3] That's exactly what GPUs are built for.

data.definition: Multiplying big grids of numbers. It's the core operation inside every neural network.

scenes.text: Why did gaming chips fit so well? [1] Games colour millions of pixels, every frame, in parallel. [2] Around 2012, researchers found the same chips could train neural networks many times faster. [3] Then, Nvidia's CUDA software made GPUs easy to program for AI.

Here are four terms. [1] VRAM, the GPU's own memory. The whole model has to fit in it. [2] Parallel processing, doing many sums at once. [3] TPU, Google's own chip made just for AI. [4] And a cluster, thousands of GPUs linked together, to train giant models.

So where do GPUs matter? [1] Training, where a big model can use thousands of GPUs for weeks. [2] Inference, every time you chat, a GPU in a data centre generates your answer. [3] And your own laptop, where a gaming GPU can run small open models.
Here's a common myth. [1] People think the fastest GPU always wins. [2] Often, memory is the real limit. If the model doesn't fit in VRAM, it won't run well, no matter how fast the chip is.

data.fact: Memory is often the real limit. If the model doesn't fit in VRAM, speed doesn't matter.
